data.content_ref: inline:The target's evolutionary analogy is self-undermining: it invokes biological natural selection as a structural justification for preferring better-corroborated theories 'based on past survival rather than future prediction,' but biological selection only produces future-adapted organisms because past survival causally determines future survival through heritable traits. This is precisely an inductive mechanism — past performance bearing on future outcomes. The target explicitly prohibits this: its own countercondition states that if the preference implies any increase in subjective probability of future success, it violates Popper's core prohibition against induction. Yet the analogy's transfer claim ('just as nature selects survivors without knowing the future, scientists select theories based on past tests') only works because in nature, past survival IS predictive of future survival via heredity. Stripped of that inductive link, natural selection would be mere random filtering with no cumulative adaptation — which the target itself lists as an overturn condition. So the analogy either (a) retains the inductive causal structure it transfers from biology, violating the countercondition, or (b) strips that structure, triggering the overturn condition and destroying the analogy. There is no coherent middle ground, making the analogy a performative contradiction of the very non-inductive stance it is meant to support.
